sentences.text: The holotype, which is the specimen the species is based on, is catalogued as MNN GDF500 and consists of a partial skeleton that lacks the skull.
The skull of Suchomimus is estimated to be about 1.2 meters long.
Suchomimus possessed a long, narrow, crocodile-like skull with sub-circular teeth that had fine to no serrations.
The dinosaur had significantly extended, blade-shaped neural spines on its vertebrae.
Neural spines suggest Suchomimus may have supported a low crest or sail of skin highest over its hips, extending further back than the sail of Spinosaurus.
Historical estimates suggest Suchomimus was 9.5 to 11 meters long and weighed between 2.5 and 3.8 metric tons.
The species Suchomimus tenerensis was described in 1998 by Paul Sereno and colleagues based on fossils found in the Elrhaz Formation.
Paul Sereno and his team discovered fossils of Suchomimus at the Gadoufaoua site in the Ténéré Desert, Niger, in late 1997.
In 1997, American paleontologist Paul Sereno and his team discovered fossils representing about two-thirds of a large theropod dinosaur skeleton in Niger.
Suchomimus was primarily a fish-eating predator adapted for hunting in shallow waters.
Researchers suggested Suchomimus was a fish-eater based on its elongated jaws, spoon-shaped snout tip, and long teeth similar to those of piscivorous crocodilians.
Isotopic evidence indicates Suchomimus relied heavily on aquatic resources, supporting a semi-aquatic foraging habit.
Suchomimus was adapted for hunting in shallow water due to hollow bones, unlike Baryonyx and Spinosaurus which could fully submerge and dive.
Suchomimus had an extensive secondary palate that would have strengthened the roof of the mouth to resist torsion forces from prey.
Suchomimus shared traits with Baryonyx, including strong forelimbs, a huge sickle-curved thumb claw, and strongly keeled front dorsal vertebrae.
Researchers have hypothesized that spinosaurid forelimbs and claws were used for digging water sources, reaching hard-to-access prey, or burrowing to build nests.
In 2005, François Therrien and colleagues hypothesized that spinosaurid forelimbs were likely used to hunt larger prey because their snouts could not withstand bending tension.
In a 2017 family review, David Hone and Holtz considered possible functions for spinosaurid forelimbs in digging for water sources, hard-to-reach prey, or excavating nests.
In its original description, Suchomimus was placed in the family Spinosauridae and assigned to the subfamily Baryonychinae.
Suchomimus is classified within the family Spinosauridae.
In 2021, Barker et al. placed Suchomimus in the new tribe Ceratosuchopsini, separate from Baryonyx, though they did not name Cristatusaurus.
Suchomimus belongs to the parent group Ceratosuchopsini.
Spinosaurids lived from approximately 130 to 95 million years ago during the Early to Late Cretaceous.
Suchomimus lived in Africa during the Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 to 112 million years ago.
Suchomimus lived over 100 million years ago in the Sahara when it was a swampy paradise.
Suchomimus lived from the Aptian to the Albian stages, between 121.4 and 100.5 million years ago.
Suchomimus shared its habitat with abundant crocodylomorphs, including the giant pholidosaur Sarcosuchus imperator and various smaller notosuchians.
Some researchers have suggested that Suchomimus is an African species of the European spinosaurid Baryonyx, leading to its occasional classification as Baryonyx tenerensis.
In 2002, Buffetaut and Ouaja supported the synonymy between Cristatusaurus and Baryonyx, noting that Suchomimus might also belong to the same genus.
It is debated whether S. tenerensis is a junior synonym of the spinosaurid Cristatusaurus lapparenti from the Elrhaz Formation.
Sereno and colleagues proposed in 1998 that spinosaurid thumb-claws and robust forelimbs evolved in the Middle Jurassic before adaptations for fish-eating appeared.
